comparisons.peer_topic: Recurring Fair Value Assets and Liabilities Summary
comparisons.peer_summary: Assets and liabilities carried at fair value on a recurring basis at December 31, 2024 and 2023 are summarized in tables, including adjustments for netting agreements and collateral, with specific inclusions for segregated securities, commodity inventory, and MSRs.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and BAC disclose that trading account assets include commodities inventory carried at the lower of cost or market/net realizable value. C states that 'Physical commodities inventory is carried at the lower of cost or market' and is part of trading activities. BAC explicitly includes 'certain commodities inventory' in its trading account assets summary, carried at the lower of cost or net realizable value. A notable difference is the materiality/amounts: BAC reports specific values ($99 million in 2024, $42 million in 2023), while C does not provide specific dollar amounts for its physical commodity inventory in this note, focusing instead on the accounting policy. Both report gains/losses on these items in Principal transactions (C explicitly states this; BAC implies it by inclusion in trading account assets which are typically marked-to-market or settled through principal transactions, though BAC's specific note focuses on the measurement basis).

Any gains and losses related to physical commodities inventory are reported in Principal transactions.

Trading account assets also includes certain commodities inventory of $99 million that is accounted for at the lower of cost or net realizable value, which is the current selling price less any costs to sell.

comparisons.peer_summary: Hybrid financial instruments containing bifurcatable embedded derivatives are either accounted for entirely at fair value under the fair value option or, if not elected, the derivative is bifurcated and accounted for at fair value while the host contract is at amortized cost.
comparisons.comparison: C and GS both discuss the accounting for hybrid financial instruments involving embedded derivatives. C specifically applies this to 'unallocated precious metals,' bifurcating the investment into a debt host and an embedded non-financial derivative, carrying both at fair value under the fair value option. GS provides the general policy for 'hybrid financial instruments,' stating they can be accounted for entirely at fair value (fair value option) or by bifurcating the embedded derivative (at fair value) from the host contract (at amortized cost). The key difference is that C elects the fair value option for its precious metal hybrids, whereas GS presents the bifurcation into amortized cost host as the alternative if the fair value option is not elected. Additionally, GS explicitly excludes physical commodities requiring physical delivery from its definition of hybrid instruments for bifurcation purposes, whereas C specifically includes unallocated precious metals (which are financial/derivative-like) in its hybrid accounting framework.

sentences.text: Investments in unallocated precious metals accounts (gold, silver, platinum and palladium) are accounted for as hybrid instruments containing a debt host contract and an embedded non-financial derivative instrument indexed to the price of the relevant precious metal.
The embedded derivative instrument and debt host contract are carried at fair value under the fair value option, as described in Note 27.
Hybrid financial instruments are instruments that contain bifurcatable embedded derivatives and do not require settlement by physical delivery of nonfinancial assets (e.g., physical commodities).

Unless the firm has elected to account for the entire hybrid financial instrument at fair value under the fair value option, the embedded derivative is bifurcated from the associated host contract, the derivative is accounted for at fair value and the host contract is accounted for at amortized cost, adjusted for the effective portion of any fair value hedges.

comparisons.peer_topic: Fair value hedge accounting for physical commodities
comparisons.peer_summary: The Firm applies fair value hedges to physical commodities inventories carried at lower of cost or net realizable value, with gains and losses recorded in principal transactions revenue.
comparisons.comparison: Both C and JPM apply the lower of cost or market/net realizable value (NRV) accounting to physical commodities inventory, with associated gains and losses recorded in Principal transactions. However, JPM explicitly states it applies fair value hedge accounting to these inventories, whereas C does not mention hedging its physical commodity inventory in this specific context but instead focuses on the accounting treatment of unallocated precious metals investments as hybrid instruments. C's disclosure includes a specific note that inventory carried at lower of cost is excluded from the fair value option when included in a hedging relationship, implying hedging exists, but JPM's disclosure is more explicit about the fair value hedge application to the inventory itself. C's unique aspect is the bifurcation of unallocated precious metals into debt hosts and embedded derivatives, a topic not present in JPM's commodity inventory disclosure.

comparisons.peer_topic: Credit Linked Notes and CDO Investments
comparisons.peer_summary: The Firm has invested in Credit Linked Notes (CLNs) and Collateralized Debt Obligations (CDOs), which are hybrid instruments containing embedded derivatives where credit protection has been sold to the issuer. If a credit event occurs for the reference entity underlying these instruments, the principal balance may not be repaid in full.
comparisons.comparison: C and MS both utilize hybrid instrument accounting for specific investments involving embedded derivatives. C accounts for unallocated precious metals as hybrid instruments with a debt host and an embedded derivative indexed to metal prices, electing fair value for both. MS accounts for Credit Linked Notes (CLNs) and CDOs as hybrid instruments containing embedded derivatives where credit protection is sold, but the disclosure does not specify the same debt host/embedded derivative bifurcation with fair value option election for the host in the same explicit manner as C for metals. MS focuses on the credit risk of the reference entity, while C focuses on the price risk of the precious metal. Both represent specialized hybrid accounting treatments for non-standard financial assets, but the underlying mechanics (commodity price vs. credit event) and specific accounting elections differ.

sentences.text: Investments in unallocated precious metals accounts (gold, silver, platinum and palladium) are accounted for as hybrid instruments containing a debt host contract and an embedded non-financial derivative instrument indexed to the price of the relevant precious metal.
The embedded derivative instrument and debt host contract are carried at fair value under the fair value option, as described in Note 27.
The Firm has invested in CLNs and CDOs, which are hybrid instruments containing embedded derivatives, in which credit protection has been sold to the issuer of the note.
If there is a credit event of a reference entity underlying the instrument, the principal balance of the note may not be repaid in full to the Firm.
